headline: Tesla Batteries Stolen from Nevada factory docks at least 11 times
summary: Millions of dollars in Powerwall systems allegedly taken before leaving Tesla's facilities, with organized groups exploiting security gaps.
details: Trailers filled with millions of dollars worth of Tesla car and home batteries have reportedly been stolen from loading docks at the company’s Nevada facilities at least 11 times since last December, according to sheriff’s records obtained by WIRED.

"It’s an epidemic right now," says Storey County Sheriff’s Detective Sam Hatley, who has been investigating the Tesla cases. Three men suspected of carrying out one of the heists were arrested in January and charged with felony possession of stolen property.

Investigators are tracking a total of 17 alleged cargo thefts this year involving Tesla and other businesses in Storey County. Some of these operations don't involve thieves snatching goods from unattended trailers; instead, organized groups have found ways to exploit gaps in security protocols, including using fake IDs.

The first of the recent cases took place in December and involved two trailers each filled with over $475,000 worth of Powerwall 3 residential battery systems. Authorities recovered the trailers empty about 500 miles away in Southern California.

Tesla's security team later found some of the Powerwalls for sale online and notified authorities. In another case, an auto parts dealer in Northern California reported being offered suspected stolen car batteries at a discount, which investigators later confirmed.

Tesla reported one additional alleged theft in December and nine more in January. One incident involved a trailer containing 123 Powerwalls destined for a Tesla facility in Hayward, California, but it never arrived. The semi-truck and driver were reportedly not licensed for interstate operations.
The car maker has since tightened its procedures, including verifying driver identities at the factory gate. "It’s definitely helping," Hatley says. Thefts are "happening, but not as prolifically."

Transportation industry researchers estimate that shipping thefts in the US roughly doubled from 2022 to 2024, costing companies nearly $18 million a day. Electronic components have been a frequent target.

headline_marked: [[AI agents are burning money]] in Next.js SaaS: 3 hidden costs of LLM calls
headline: AI agents are burning money in Next.js SaaS: 3 hidden costs of LLM calls
summary: Many Next.js SaaS projects leveraging AI agents face unexpected cost overruns from LLM calls, often leading to project shutdowns despite successful implementation.
details: AI agents, while effective in automating tasks, can incur prohibitive costs when integrated into Next.js SaaS applications, leading to projects being shut down. One such pipeline, designed to rewrite job descriptions at scale, was killed due to the unexpected bill from GPT-class models.

The common focus on accuracy, latency, and user experience often overlooks the critical fourth dimension: 'cost per action'. This oversight in AI agent architecture is a primary reason why many AI features fail to survive their first billing cycle.

Three key patterns contribute to these escalating costs: redundant context resends, a lack of caching strategies, and the indiscriminate use of expensive LLMs for all tasks. These issues collectively inflate operational expenses significantly.

Redundant context resends occur when the same system prompt is sent repeatedly across parallel agent calls, wasting gigabytes of tokens hourly at scale. Without caching, identical or nearly identical LLM calls are paid for at full price every time. Furthermore, using powerful models like GPT-4 for simple classification or extraction tasks is inefficient when cheaper alternatives suffice.

Effective solutions begin with prompt caching. Caching system prompts can prevent hundreds of thousands of tokens from being wasted by avoiding repeated sends, a simple fix often overlooked until billing issues become critical. This strategy works with most LLM providers, including OpenAI and Anthropic.

Implementing a two-tier routing approach allows simple tasks to be handled by cheaper, specialized models, while complex tasks are routed to more powerful, expensive ones. This alone can make a significant difference; for example, DeepSeek V4 Flash can be 23x cheaper than GPT-4 for certain tasks while maintaining sufficient quality.

Preventing retries is another crucial cost-saving measure. Utilizing function calling with strict JSON schemas ensures that models return valid data or fail cleanly, eliminating costly regeneration loops caused by malformed output or hallucinations. Every avoided retry directly translates to saved operational costs.

Ultimately, successful teams treat cost as a first-class constraint in their AI agent architecture. They design systems with aggressive caching, intelligent routing, and robust output validation to manage budgets effectively, ensuring their AI features remain viable and sustainable.
